title: The ENTIRE History of the Ottoman Empire in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of the Ottoman Empire in 10 Minutes
description:
From a tiny frontier state in 1299 to the last sultan sailing away in 1922, this is the whole story of the Ottoman Empire in about ten minutes: Osman's legendary dream, ships dragged over a hill to take Constantinople, Suleiman the Magnificent, princes locked in 'the Cage', a sultan who banned coffee, soldiers who revolted by flipping soup pots, the 1683 charge at Vienna, the 'sick man of Europe' and the birth of modern Turkey. Every fact is checked, and legends are labelled as legends.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #ottomanempire #ottoman #turkey #animatedhistory

beats.say: April 1453. The young Ottoman sultan, Mehmed the Second, has a problem.
He wants Constantinople, the thousand-year-old capital of what's left of the Roman Empire. But a giant floating chain blocks its harbor, the Golden Horn, so his ships can't get in.
Can't sail through the chain? Fine. We'll sail over the hill.
And he did. His men laid a road of greased logs. They dragged about seventy ships over the hill and slid them into the harbor, behind the chain.
About five weeks later, Constantinople fell. The Ottomans had started as a tiny frontier state. Now they were on their way to becoming a giant empire.
How did they get here? Let's go back.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of the Ottoman Empire in 10 Minutes

show.title: A Tiny State With Big Dreams

beats.say: Around 1300, Anatolia, the big peninsula that's now Turkey, was split into little Turkish states called beyliks.
One of the smallest belonged to a warrior chief named Osman. It sat right on the border of the Byzantine Empire, the last piece of the old Roman Empire.

tag.text: Osman I, founder of the dynasty

beats.say: Being on the border was great for business. And business, here, mostly meant raiding.
Later Ottoman writers told a legend about him. Osman slept at the home of a holy man, Sheikh Edebali. He dreamed a moon rose from the sheikh's chest and sank into his own.
Then a giant tree sprouted from Osman's belly button, and its shade covered the whole world.
It means your family will rule a great empire. Also, you may marry my daughter.
Wonderful. But is my belly button okay?
That story was written down over a hundred years after Osman died. But his name stuck. Osman, or Othman, gave us the word Ottoman.
Later Ottoman historians picked 1299 as the year it all began. And the empire would last more than six centuries.

show.label: The Ottoman Empire lasted about
show.sub: 1299 to 1922, one family the whole time

beats.say: In 1326, Osman's son Orhan captured the rich city of Bursa and made it his capital.
In the 1350s, the Ottomans crossed into Europe. Soon they held land on both sides of Constantinople.

show.title: Cannons, Ships and a New Capital

beats.say: That left Constantinople like an island, surrounded by Ottoman land. In 1451, an eighteen-year-old named Mehmed became sultan, and he wanted that city.
He hired a cannon maker named Orban to build monster guns. The biggest one reportedly needed about sixty oxen to drag it.
Then came the chain, the hill and the seventy ships. On May 29, 1453, after a fifty-three-day siege, Ottoman troops broke through the walls.
The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine the Eleventh, died in the fighting. After almost fifteen hundred years, the Roman Empire was over.
Mehmed made the city his new capital, the city we now call Istanbul. Its great church, Hagia Sophia, became a mosque.
He also built a brand-new palace, Topkapı. Sultans lived there for almost four hundred years.
Next, Mehmed's grandson Selim conquered Egypt, Syria, and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. It took him about two years.
Then, in 1520, his son took over. Meet Suleiman. Europeans called him the Magnificent. At home he was the Lawgiver, because he organized the empire's laws.
And he stayed on the throne. For a very long time.

show.label: Suleiman ruled for
show.sub: 1520 to 1566, the longest of any Ottoman sultan

beats.say: In 1526, his army smashed the Hungarians at Mohács. In 1529, he marched all the way to Vienna and besieged it.
But autumn came, it rained and rained, and his army was a very long way from home. So he gave up and went back.
At sea, Suleiman made a famous corsair, a sea raider nicknamed Barbarossa, or Red Beard, his top admiral. In 1538, Barbarossa beat a bigger Christian fleet at Preveza, in Greece.
I hear you used to be a pirate.
A privateer, Your Majesty. That's a pirate with paperwork.
On land, Suleiman's architect, Sinan, built the giant Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul. Sinan's team put up more than three hundred major buildings.
By Suleiman's death, the empire stretched across three continents. It ran from Hungary to Iraq, and from Algeria to the Red Sea.
After Suleiman, palace life got weird. Early on, a new sultan often had his brothers executed, so none could fight him for the throne.
In the 1600s, that changed. Spare princes were kept alive, but locked away in a palace apartment nicknamed the Kafes, which means the Cage.
One prince, Suleiman the Second, spent nearly forty years in there. When soldiers came to make him sultan in 1687, he was terrified.
If you've come to kill me, just say so.
Kill you? No! You're the sultan now!
With rulers raised like that, who actually ran things? Often, their mothers.
Kösem Sultan was the mother of two sultans. In 1623, her son Murad took the throne at age eleven, so she governed for him as regent.
You're eleven, dear. Mother will handle the empire.
Royal mothers and wives were so powerful in this era that historians call it the Sultanate of Women.
Murad grew up tough. In 1633, a huge fire, blamed on a careless smoker, burned a big part of Istanbul.
So Murad banned tobacco and coffee, and closed the coffeehouses, where men gossiped about the government. Chroniclers say he prowled the streets at night in disguise.
Mmm. Is that coffee I smell?
Coffee? No, sir. This is just very, very dark soup.
Rule-breakers could be executed. But after Murad died, the bans faded, and Istanbul went right back to coffee.
Speaking of soup: the Janissaries were the sultan's elite foot soldiers. They gave their officers kitchen titles, like soup maker and head cook.
And when they were angry, they flipped over their big soup pots. That was the signal for a revolt. In 1622, rebel Janissaries even overthrew a young sultan.
In 1683, the grand vizier, the sultan's chief minister, marched a giant army back to Vienna. His name was Kara Mustafa Pasha.
For two months, Ottoman diggers tunneled under the city walls, while the people inside ran low on food.
Then, on September 12, a rescue army arrived, led by the Polish king, Jan Sobieski.

tag.text: King Jan III Sobieski of Poland

beats.say: His winged hussars were horsemen with tall feathered frames on their backs. They led what's often called the biggest cavalry charge in history. About eighteen thousand riders poured down the hill.
The Ottoman army broke and fled. In 1699, at the Treaty of Karlowitz, the empire gave up most of Hungary. Historians see this as the moment it started shrinking for good.
The court cheered itself up with flowers. Rich officials paid fortunes for rare tulips. Historians later named the years 1718 to 1730 the Tulip Era.
By the mid-1800s, the empire flew this red flag with a star and crescent. But it was falling behind Europe's new factories and armies.
In 1826, Sultan Mahmud the Second shut down the Janissaries for good and built a modern army.
Next came big reforms called the Tanzimat, meaning reorganization. They brought new schools, new courts, and equal rights for all religions, at least on paper.
But Russia smelled weakness. In January 1853, Tsar Nicholas the First chatted with the British ambassador about the Ottomans.
The ambassador, Sir Hamilton Seymour, reported his words.

show.text: We have on our hands a sick man—a very sick man.
show.who: Tsar Nicholas I, as reported by British ambassador Sir Hamilton Seymour, 1853

beats.say: So, when he dies, shall we split up his things?
Britain would rather he got better, thank you.
Britain and France wanted the sick man alive, to keep Russia out. So in the Crimean War, from 1853 to 1856, they fought on the Ottoman side, and won.
But the nickname stuck. Over the next sixty years, the empire lost Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria and almost all its land in Europe.
In 1914, the Ottomans joined World War One, on the side of Germany.
In 1915, Allied troops from Britain, France, Australia and New Zealand landed at Gallipoli, hoping to reach Istanbul. A young Ottoman officer, Mustafa Kemal, helped hold them off.
After eight months of fighting, the Allies gave up and left.
Now the tone of our story has to change. Starting in 1915, the Ottoman government forced Armenians, a Christian people of the empire, from their homes.
Somewhere between six hundred thousand and over a million Armenians were killed or died on forced marches. Historians call it the Armenian Genocide.
In 1918, the Ottomans lost the war. Allied warships sailed into Istanbul, and the winners planned to carve up what was left.

tag.text: Sultan Mehmed VI, the last sultan

beats.say: Mustafa Kemal led a war of independence from Ankara, and won. On November 1, 1922, his new parliament abolished the sultanate.
Sixteen days later, the last sultan, Mehmed the Sixth, quietly left Istanbul on a British warship.
In 1923, Kemal declared the Republic of Turkey, with Ankara as its capital. He later took the surname Atatürk, Father of the Turks.
So a border chief's tiny state became an empire on three continents. One family ruled it for over six hundred years. Not bad for a guy with a tree in his belly button.
